title: Physics-Informed Broad Learning System: An Efficient Backpropagation-Free Framework for Solving Partial Differential Equations

3.1 Broad Learning System


In this subsection, we present the architecture of the BLS. Let {(X,Y)|X∈ℝN×m,Y∈ℝN}\{(X,Y)|X\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m},\,Y\in\mathbb{R}^{N}\} be the training dataset, where X∈ℝN×mX\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times m} is the input matrix and Y∈ℝNY\in\mathbb{R}^{N} is the output matrix.


The BLS is composed of three key components: (1) mapping feature nodes, (2) enhancement feature nodes, and (3) the output matrix. The training process of the BLS involves two main stages. First, the weights for both the mapping and enhancement nodes are randomly generated, eliminating the need for iterative tuning in these layers. Second, the weights connecting the hidden layer to the output layer are computed analytically, typically using a least-squares solution. In essence, only the final output weights are learned during training, while the rest of the network remains fixed. This significantly reduces computational cost and training time.


Figure 1: Architecture of the BLS


The architecture of the BLS [6] is shown in Figure 1. Let there be NcN_{c} feature layers, each consisting of pp nodes. For the ithi^{\text{th}} feature layer, let Wif∈ℝm×pW_{i}^{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times p} and bif∈ℝ1×pb_{i}^{f}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{1\times p} denote the randomly generated weight matrix and bias vector, respectively. The output of the ithi^{\text{th}} feature layer is then defined as:




Fi=ψi​(X​Wif+𝟏T⊗bif)∈ℝN×p,i=1,2,…,Nc,\displaystyle F^{i}=\psi_{i}(XW_{i}^{f}+\bm{1}^{T}\otimes b_{i}^{f})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times p},\quad i=1,2,\ldots,N_{c},

(3.1)


where 𝟏∈ℝN\bm{1}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N} is the vector of all ones and ψi\psi_{i} is the activation function (feature mapping) associated with the ithi^{\text{th}} feature group, applied elementwise to the matrix 𝐅​Wif+bif\mathbf{F}W_{i}^{f}+b_{i}^{f}. The symbol ⊗\otimes denotes the Kronecker product. The following augmented matrix gives the output of the feature group:




𝐅=[F1F2…FNc]∈ℝN×p​Nc.\displaystyle\mathbf{F}=\left[\begin{matrix}F^{1}&F^{2}&\ldots&F^{N_{c}}\end{matrix}\right]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times pN_{c}}.

(3.2)




In the next step, the augmented feature matrix is projected into the enhancement space through random transformations, followed by the application of activation functions. Let
NeN_{e} denote the number of enhancement layers, with each group consisting of
qq nodes. Further, let Wie∈ℝp​Nc×qW_{i}^{e}\in\mathbb{R}^{pN_{c}\times q} be the randomly generated weight matrix connecting the feature matrix 𝐅\mathbf{F} to the ithi^{\text{th}} enhancement group, and let bie∈ℝ1×qb_{i}^{e}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{1\times q} denote the corresponding bias vector for the ithi^{\text{th}} enhancement group.
Then




Ei=ϕi​(𝐅​Wie+𝟏⊗bie)∈ℝN×q,i=1,2,…,Ne,\displaystyle E^{i}=\phi_{i}(\mathbf{F}W_{i}^{e}+\bm{1}\otimes b_{i}^{e})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times q},\quad i=1,2,\ldots,N_{e},

(3.3)


where ϕi\phi_{i} is the activation function used to generate nonlinear
features, applied elementwise to the matrix 𝐅​Wje+bje\mathbf{F}W_{j}^{e}+b_{j}^{e}. The output of the NeN_{e} enhancement feature groups is




𝐄=[E1E2…ENe]∈ℝN×q​Ne.\displaystyle\mathbf{E}=\left[\begin{matrix}E^{1}&E^{2}&\ldots&E^{N_{e}}\end{matrix}\right]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times qN_{e}}.

(3.4)


Finally, the resulting enhancement matrix 𝐄\mathbf{E}, together with the augmented feature matrix 𝐅\mathbf{F}, is passed to the output layer, where the resulting output of the network is computed as follows:




Y^=𝒢​Wu,\displaystyle\widehat{Y}=\mathcal{G}W_{u},

(3.5)


where 𝒢=[𝐅𝐄]∈ℝN×(p​Nc+q​Ne)\mathcal{G}=\left[\begin{matrix}\mathbf{F}&\mathbf{E}\end{matrix}\right]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{N\times(pN_{c}+qN_{e})} denotes the concatenated matrix of the augmented feature layer and the resultant enhancement layer, and Wu∈ℝ(p​Nc+q​Ne)×1W_{u}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{(pN_{c}+qN_{e})\times 1}
is the randomly generated weight matrix that connects this combined representation to the output layer.
Finally, the training of the BLS is completed by estimating the output weight matrix through the following least-squares optimization problem:




minWu⁡‖𝒢​Wu−Y‖22.\min_{W_{u}}\;\|\mathcal{G}W_{u}-Y\|_{2}^{2}.

(3.6)

3.2 Physics-Informed Neural Network


Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are a class of machine learning methods that incorporate domain-specific knowledge, typically represented by PDEs—into the neural network training process. The central idea of PINNs is to embed the governing physical laws as constraints, ensuring that the neural network’s predictions adhere to the underlying system dynamics during training.


Figure 2: Framework of PINN


We consider the following form of a general PDE:





∂∂t​𝒖​(𝒙,t)+𝒩𝒙​[𝒖​(𝒙,t)]=R​(𝒙,t),𝒙∈Ω,and​t∈[0,T]\displaystyle\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\bm{u}(\bm{x},t)+\mathcal{N}_{\bm{x}}[\bm{u}(\bm{x},t)]=R(\bm{x},t),\penalty 10000\ \penalty 10000\ \bm{x}\in\Omega,\penalty 10000\ \text{and}\penalty 10000\ t\in[0,T]

(3.7)




ℬ​[𝒖​(𝒙,t)]=B​(𝒙,t),𝒙∈∂Ω,and​t∈[0,T],\displaystyle\mathcal{B}[\bm{u}(\bm{x},t)]=B(\bm{x},t),\penalty 10000\ \penalty 10000\ \bm{x}\in\partial\Omega,\penalty 10000\ \text{and}\penalty 10000\ t\in[0,\,T],

(3.8)




𝒖​(𝒙,0)=ℐ​(𝒙),𝒙∈Ω,\displaystyle\bm{u}(\bm{x},0)=\mathcal{I}(\bm{x}),\penalty 10000\ \bm{x}\in\Omega,

(3.9)


where 𝒙∈ℝd\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d}, t∈[0,T],t\in[0,\,T], and 𝒩𝒙​[𝒖]\mathcal{N}_{\bm{x}}[\bm{u}] and ℬ​[𝒖]\mathcal{B}[\bm{u}] are the potentially nonlinear differential operator and the boundary condition operator, respectively, and ∂Ω\partial\Omega is the boundary of the computation domain Ω.\Omega.


The framework for PINN is given in Figure 2. The PINN is employed to approximate the
solution 𝒖​(x,t)\bm{u}(x,t) by 𝒖~​(x,t)\widetilde{\bm{u}}(x,t), where the network takes (𝒙,t)(\bm{x},t) as inputs. Let the collocation points at the interior of the domain be denoted by {𝒙i,u,ti,u}i=1Nc\{\bm{x}_{i,u},t_{i,u}\}_{i=1}^{N_{c}}, the boundary points by {𝒙i,b,ti,b}i=1Nb\{\bm{x}_{i,b},t_{i,b}\}_{i=1}^{N_{b}}, and the initial points {𝒙i,I,0}i=1NI\{\bm{x}_{i,I},0\}_{i=1}^{N_{I}}, where Nu,N_{u}, NbN_{b} and NIN_{I} denote the number of training collocation points, boundary points, and initial condition points, respectively. The residuals associated with the PDE, boundary conditions, and initial conditions are denoted by 𝒥u,\mathcal{J}_{u}, 𝒥b,\mathcal{J}_{b}, and 𝒥I,\mathcal{J}_{I}, respectively, and given as follows:





𝒥u​(𝒙,t)=∂𝒖~∂t​(𝒙,t)+𝒩𝒙​[𝒖~]​(𝒙,t)−R​(𝒙,t)on{𝒙i,u,ti,u}i=1Nc,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{u}(\bm{x},t)=\frac{\partial\widetilde{\bm{u}}}{\partial t}(\bm{x},t)+\mathcal{N}_{\bm{x}}[\widetilde{\bm{u}}](\bm{x},t)-{R}(\bm{x},t)\penalty 10000\ \penalty 10000\ \text{on}\penalty 10000\ \penalty 10000\ \{\bm{x}_{i,u},t_{i,u}\}_{i=1}^{N_{c}},

(3.10)




𝒥b​(𝒙,t)=ℬ​[𝒖~]​(𝒙,t)−B​(𝒙,t)on{𝒙i,b,ti,b}i=1Nb,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{b}(\bm{x},t)=\mathcal{B}[\widetilde{\bm{u}}](\bm{x},t)-{B}(\bm{x},t)\penalty 10000\ \penalty 10000\ \text{on}\penalty 10000\ \penalty 10000\ \{\bm{x}_{i,b},t_{i,b}\}_{i=1}^{N_{b}},

(3.11)




𝒥I​(𝒙,0)=𝒖~​(𝒙,0)−ℐ​(𝒙)on{𝒙i,I,0}iNI.\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{I}(\bm{x},0)=\widetilde{\bm{u}}(\bm{x},0)-\mathcal{I}(\bm{x})\penalty 10000\ \penalty 10000\ \text{on}\penalty 10000\ \penalty 10000\ \{\bm{x}_{i,I},0\}_{i}^{N_{I}}.

(3.12)


Therefore, the loss terms due to the PDE, boundary conditions, and initial conditions, respectively, are given by





𝒥u=∑i=1Nc|∂𝒖~∂t​(𝒙i,u,ti,u)+𝒩𝒙​[𝒖~​(𝒙i,u,ti,u)]−R​(𝒙i,u,ti,u)|2,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{u}=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{c}}\left|\frac{\partial\widetilde{\bm{u}}}{\partial t}(\bm{x}_{i,u},t_{i,u})+\mathcal{N}_{\bm{x}}[\widetilde{\bm{u}}(\bm{x}_{i,u},t_{i,u})]-R(\bm{x}_{i,u},t_{i,u})\right|^{2},

(3.13)




𝒥b=∑i=1Nb|ℬ​[𝒖~]​(𝒙i,b,ti,b)−B​(𝒙i,b,ti,b)|2,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{b}=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{b}}\left|\mathcal{B}[\widetilde{\bm{u}}](\bm{x}_{i,b},t_{i,b})-B(\bm{x}_{i,b},t_{i,b})\right|^{2},

(3.14)




𝒥I=∑i=1NI|𝒖~​(𝒙i,I,0)−ℐ​(𝒙i,I)|2.\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{I}=\sum_{i=1}^{N_{I}}\left|\widetilde{\bm{u}}(\bm{x}_{i,I},0)-\mathcal{I}(\bm{x}_{i,I})\right|^{2}.

(3.15)


Accordingly, the total loss to be minimized for a PINN is given by:




𝒥:=12​Nu​𝒥u+12​Nb​𝒥b+12​NI​𝒥b.\displaystyle\mathcal{J}:=\frac{1}{2N_{u}}\mathcal{J}_{u}+\frac{1}{2N_{b}}\mathcal{J}_{b}+\frac{1}{2N_{I}}\mathcal{J}_{b}.

(3.16)


The partial derivatives involved in the loss function can be efficiently computed using automatic differentiation [1, 27].
By applying a gradient-based optimization algorithm, we can minimize the loss function 𝒥\mathcal{J} to determine the optimal weights and biases of the neural network.

4 Proposed Physics-Informed Broad Learning System


In this section, we introduce the physics-informed broad learning system (PI-BLS), which integrates the principles of PINNs with BLS to solve linear PDEs. The core idea is to incorporate physical laws directly into the BLS framework as part of the cost function. This transforms linear PDE problems into a regularized linear least-squares problem, allowing the solution to simultaneously satisfy the governing equations and boundary/initial conditions in a computationally efficient manner. In the following, we discuss the mathematical architecture of PI-BLS.


Consider the general PDE problem (3.7)-(3.9). The architecture of the PI-BLS is shown in Figure 3.
Define X=[𝒙T,t]∈ℝ1×(d+1),X=[\bm{x}^{T},\,t]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{1\times(d+1)}, where 𝒙∈ℝd\bm{x}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{d} and t∈ℝt\in{\mathbb{R}}. Let the network have NfN_{f} feature layers with pp feature nodes in each layer. The feature layers are denoted by Fi,F^{i}, i=1,2,…,Nci=1,2,\ldots,N_{c}. Further, let Wif∈ℝ(d+1)×pW^{f}_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{(d+1)\times p} be the weight matrix and bif∈ℝ1×pb^{f}_{i}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{1\times p} be the biases in the it​hi^{th} feature layer. Then the output of the feature layer segment is given by




F=[F1F2…FNc]∈ℝ1×p​Nc,\displaystyle\textbf{F}=\left[\begin{matrix}F^{1}&F^{2}&\ldots&F^{N_{c}}\end{matrix}\right]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{1\times pN_{c}},

(4.1)


where Fi​(X)=ψi​(X​Wif+bif)∈ℝ1×pF^{i}(X)=\psi_{i}(XW^{f}_{i}+b_{i}^{f})\in{\mathbb{R}}^{1\times p} is the output in the it​hi^{th} physics-informed feature layer, and ψi:ℝ→ℝ\psi_{i}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} are the feature maps or nonlinear activation functions.


Figure 3: Framework of the proposed PI-BLS


Let the network consist of NeN_{e} enhancement layers, each containing qq enhancement nodes. These enhancement layers are denoted by EjE^{j}, for j=1,2,…,Nej=1,2,\ldots,N_{e}. Let Wje∈ℝp​Nc×qW^{e}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{pN_{c}\times q} be the weight matrix and bje∈ℝ1×qb^{e}_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times q} be the bias vector in the jthj^{\text{th}} enhancement layer. Then, the output of the enhancement layer is given by:






E=[E1E2…ENe]∈ℝ1×q​Ne,\displaystyle\textbf{E}=\left[\begin{matrix}E^{1}&E^{2}&\ldots&E^{N_{e}}\end{matrix}\right]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{1\times qN_{e}},

(4.2)


where




Ej​(X)=ϕj​(𝐅​Wje+bje)∈ℝ1×q,E^{j}(X)=\phi_{j}(\mathbf{F}W_{j}^{e}+b_{j}^{e})\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times q},



with ϕj:ℝ→ℝ\phi_{j}:\mathbb{R}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} being nonlinear activation functions.
The final output of the network denoted by 𝒖~\widetilde{\bm{u}} and is given by




𝒖~​(X;Wu)=𝒢​W𝒖,\displaystyle\widetilde{\bm{u}}(X;W_{u})=\mathcal{G}W_{\bm{u}},

(4.3)


where 𝒢=[𝑭​𝑬]∈ℝ1×(p​Nc+q​Ne)\mathcal{G}=[\bm{F}\,\penalty 10000\ \bm{E}]\in{\mathbb{R}}^{1\times(pN_{c}+qN_{e})} and W𝒖∈ℝ(p​Nc+q​Ne)×1.W_{\bm{u}}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{(pN_{c}+qN_{e})\times 1}. Hence, 𝒖~​(X;Wu)\widetilde{\bm{u}}(X;W_{u}) is the approximate solution of the PDE (3.7)–(3.9) obtained using the network.


Let Nu,N_{u}, NbN_{b}, and NIN_{I} denote the numbers of collocation points, boundary points, and initial conditions, respectively, due to training. The error functions in approximating the PDE, boundary conditions, and initial conditions are the same as in (3.10), (3.11), and (3.12).
Hence, the loss functions to be minimized for a PI-BLS are given by:

(4.4)



𝒥b​(𝒙,t)=ℬ​[𝒢​Wu]​(𝒙,t)−B​(𝒙,t)on{𝒙i,b,ti,b}i=1Nb,\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{b}(\bm{x},t)=\mathcal{B}[\mathcal{G}W_{u}](\bm{x},t)-{B}(\bm{x},t)\penalty 10000\ \penalty 10000\ \text{on}\penalty 10000\ \penalty 10000\ \{\bm{x}_{i,b},t_{i,b}\}_{i=1}^{N_{b}},

(4.5)

(4.6)

Xcol=[(𝒙1,u,t1,u),(𝒙2,u,t2,u),…,(𝒙Nu,u,tNu,u)]T,X_{\mathrm{col}}=[(\bm{x}_{1,u},t_{1,u}),(\bm{x}_{2,u},t_{2,u}),\ldots,(\bm{x}_{N_{u},u},t_{N_{u},u})]^{T},

𝒪​(Nu​Nh2+Nh3)\mathcal{O}\!\left(N_{u}N_{h}^{2}+N_{h}^{3}\right)






The computational complexity of the proposed PI-BLS framework is compared with those of PINN, and RdNN-based physics-informed extreme learning machine (PI-ELM) [9], and Bayesian PI-ELM (B-PI-ELM) [20]. Let NuN_{u} denote the total number of collocation points, including interior, boundary, and initial points. For PINN, let LhL_{h} and NhN_{h} denote the number of hidden layers and hidden nodes per layer, respectively, and let TT denote the total number of optimization iterations. For PI-BLS, let M=p​Nc+q,M=pN_{c}+q, where Ne=1N_{e}=1, Nc×pN_{c}\times p represents the total number of mapped feature nodes, and qq denotes the number of enhancement nodes.
For a conventional PINN, the dominant computational cost arises from repeated forward propagation and backpropagation over all trainable parameters during each optimization iteration. Assuming a fully connected network, the overall training complexity can be approximated as
𝒪PINN=𝒪​(T​Nu​Lh​Nh2)\mathcal{O}_{\text{PINN}}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(TN_{u}L_{h}N_{h}^{2}\right).
In contrast, the hidden-layer parameters of PI-BLS remain fixed after random initialization, and only the output-layer weights are estimated through a regularized least-squares problem. The computational cost consists of constructing the hidden-layer output matrix, forming the normal equations, and solving the resulting linear system, yielding
𝒪PI-BLS=𝒪​(Nu​M2+M3)\mathcal{O}_{\text{PI-BLS}}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(N_{u}M^{2}+M^{3}\right).
Similarly, both PI-ELM and B-PI-ELM employ randomized hidden layers and determine the output weights through linear least-squares optimization. Their dominant computational complexity is therefore given by
𝒪PI-ELM=𝒪B-PI-ELM=𝒪​(Nu​Nh2+Nh3)\mathcal{O}_{\text{PI-ELM}}=\mathcal{O}_{\text{B-PI-ELM}}=\mathcal{O}\!\left(N_{u}N_{h}^{2}+N_{h}^{3}\right).


The computational complexities of all competing methods are summarized in Table 1. It can be observed that the complexity of PINN scales linearly with the number of optimization iterations, making the training process considerably more expensive for large-scale problems. In contrast, PI-BLS, PI-ELM, and B-PI-ELM require only a single least-squares optimization, eliminating iterative backpropagation altogether. Consequently, PI-BLS achieves computational complexity of the same order as PI-ELM and B-PI-ELM while maintaining a richer broad learning architecture.
